title: Princess Charlene of Monaco joins royal houses in a grand farewell to King Harald V - HOLA
content: The Nordic country is preparing for its largest security operation in recent memory to honor the man who reigned over the nation for the last thirty-five years. On September 9, leading members of Europe’s royal families will gather at Oslo Cathedral to bid farewell to King Harald V of Norway in a grand ceremony that will highlight the shared ties among each of the reigning dynasties in attendance. Now, just days after it was confirmed that Prince Albert II would attend as Monaco’s representative, Princess Charlene has joined this powerful show of unity that aims to underline an exceptional reign. The news was confirmed by the Princely Palace of Monaco in a detailed statement announcing the Princess’s attendance. Oslo Cathedral will become the most important royal stage of our century to pay full honors to the late Norwegian monarch, who passed away on August 28. His death led to the automatic accession of the then crown prince as king of the country, under the name Haakon VIII. He will now reign alongside Queen Mette-Marit, forming a new royal couple at the head of the dynasty. The King’s passing has left one of the most significant marks in recent times, which will inevitably be reflected in the profound respect shown by each of the reigning royal houses. With the guest list now complete for the state funeral set for September 9th,  Prince Albert and Princess Charlene have joined the long list of dignitaries traveling to the Nordic country to say goodbye to King Harald. Princess Charlene, who does not often travel abroad with Prince Albert, is making a rare exception for one of the most notable events of our century, not only because the figure being honored is a monarch who reigned for nearly four decades, but also because Europe’s royal families, though no longer bound by the strictest of court protocols, still preserve deep dynastic ties that now translate into lasting support. The statement released by the Monegasque court also made it clear that the tributes to the late King would go beyond their presence at the state funeral. “His Serene Highness the Prince has ordered that the flags of the Prince’s Palace and public buildings be flown at half-mast on Wednesday, September 9, from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., as a sign of the solidarity and friendship that unite the Kingdom of Norway and the Principality, as well as their attachment to the historic and diplomatic ties that bind them.” A moving tribute in which royal family members from across Europe will come together to bid a final farewell to Harald V. The presence of so many royals in the Nordic capital, along with gestures of mourning in places as far away as the Principality of Monaco, reaffirms the bonds between Europe’s reigning monarchies. Their respect is now directed not only toward the late king, who wore the crown for more than three decades, but also toward the man now facing one of the greatest institutional challenges in Norway’s history: Haakon VIII, the new king, who will welcome world leaders as they gather once again in the fresh air of the Nordic capital. © ¡HOLA! title: Fanta: Western Michigan 'deserved' win v. Michigan - Yahoo Sports
content: Upon request by a viewer voicemail, John Fanta and Jay Croucher unpack the controversial ending to Western Michigan's heartbreaking loss to Michigan and explain why the Broncos "deserved" to get a program-defining win. Folks, what happened over the weekend though, on Saturday, is where we are going to begin. Because what happened on Saturday was wild at The Big House. J.J. Buchanan with a catch on a Hail Mary, as time expired, after a second was put back on the clock. My favorite team for college football is the Michigan Wolverines. Last night I watched them play Western Michigan, and it reminded me of my first game ever as a fan, when I was just a young boy, when they played Appalachian State to open the season. But listen man, I have an 11-month-old at home, and he came up to me crying. And he said to me, "Dad, I've never seen such a grave miscarry of justice, and I, I just don't know what to do." John, my question to you is, what advice should I give my son, considering that despite the fact that our team won, they were the complete beneficiary of an absolute shaft job- Well- to a lesser talent team that should've won the game. The deal is, what happened there on Saturday, it was, it was unlike anything I, I think w- we've ever seen, I've ever seen watching football for 31 years. The, the thing that comes to mind, and Jeff, I appreciate the call. And with, and with your, 11-month-old son, he's certainly learning the English language there quickly. But I, I think what I take away from this game, is, is three things. Number one, your heart breaks for Western Michigan. For those kids, they thought they had a, their greatest win in school history, Jay. And, they, they were, they were denied of that, and you've gotta try to bat that pass down, but, but they were unable to. And, but the fact is, Western Michigan deserved to win the game. They outplayed Michigan, they out-muscled Michigan, all of that. As the clock expires on the, on the first attempt for the Hail Mary, our entire crew, you know, that was, that, was watching the game like all of you were watching the game, you, you just naturally think to yourself, "Well, that is the game." And I think that, you know, we're so used to watching NFL games where these types of things have happened, and that, that is the football game. Had they never looked at, anything, had they never looked at, at anything, would we be talking about any sort of clock issue or any sort of clock, potential situation? What in the heck is Michigan doing only beating Western Michigan 13 to 12? Bryce Underwood, Bryce Underwood is, to me, not gonna be the starting quarterback for the Michigan Wolverines for much longer. I think you might see two Carrs in college football. Carr and the backup at Michigan, the other grandson of Lloyd Carr, Tommy Carr is the backup, Jay. Bryce Underwood was the number one player out of his high school class. And he has looked the furthest thing from that- Yeah thus far, in his career. But, it, it was about as catastrophic of a victory as you can possibly have. I think it's really interesting that Michigan, they were going to be two and a half point favorites against Oklahoma, they're now five and a half point underdogs, which shows what the market thinks of Michigan. Well, the other thing too is that, and this is very niche. For everything that happened in that game, what I take away from it, as a, a Hail Mary connoisseur, I hate when teams only rush three on a Hail Mary, because I just think that that is just a recipe for letting the quarterback set up and plant their feet and do whatever they wanna do. But watching those two plays back, the Hail Mary that didn't work, th- only three were sent, and then Western Michigan did actually send four on the Hail Mary that connected, and they sent the pressure, which is usually what I like in a Hail Mary, just didn't work out. A loss for a lot of different, people, a lot of different, elements to that. But yeah, also a loss for, the four-man rush on a Hail Mary. What advice do, do I have for Jeff's 11-month-old son? Maybe, maybe, I, you're too, it's too late to not follow in dad's footsteps. My son's stuck with Cleveland sports, so I can't steer you from that. Was it ever a thought to not have your son follow Cleveland sports? You have a, you have an eight-year-old, a six-year-old, right? Yeah, so they're- And their sports fandom's determined by them or by you? It's determined Well, the thing is, is like we live near Yankee Stadium so we're gonna be Yankees fans, which I'm sure will be a great source of banter, over the course of the show. But yeah, we're open for a football team probably between the Jets and the Giants. I think the only other thing I'd say is, you hope that spinning it ahead for, for all of college football, that if, if we're going to have this type of thing, you know, or, or type of review ever happen again, and we need tenths of a second- Yeah like basketball has, why not? Why, why not try to get things as correct, as possible? I think if I'm Kyle Whittingham, when I went to bed the other night in Ann Arbor, I'm saying to myself, "What did I get myself involved with here?" Because now you're at the center of attention, you're the center of the sports world. You know, he could've rode off into the sunset, and now he's got this on his hands. He's making a lot of money, making a lot of money, but he's dealing with a lot of stress here because Michigan expects to be a playoff team. They don't even look like fourth or fifth best in the Big 10 right now.

title: Remembering Eugene V. Debs this Labor Day - WTHI-TV
content: TERRE HAUTE, Ind. (WTHI) - Eugene V. Debs, a pioneer for the American labor movement, was born right here in Terre Haute, and community members are working to keep his memory alive. As the nation celebrates Labor Day, local historians and museum advocates are pointing back to Debs’ lasting impact on the American worker. “Labor Day is actually a thing in part because of Eugene Debs,” said Allison Duerk, director of the Eugene V. Debs Museum. “And it was his union, the American Railway Union, that led the Pullman Strike of 1894.” Debs was a passionate social activist who advocated tirelessly for fair working conditions, safety, and livable wages. His efforts often came at a massive personal cost. “He spearheaded what was a movement for workers, and it’s not typical,” said Lisa Phillips with the Eugene V. Debs Foundation. The historic Pullman Strike of 1894 paralyzed rail traffic across the nation and ultimately led to federal intervention. “Debs and the union’s officers ended up in jail, and we got Labor Day out of the deal,” Duerk explained. In 1962, the Terre Haute home of Debs and his wife, Katherine, was turned into a museum to preserve his memory and teach future generations about his national impact. This year holds extraordinary significance for the museum and the foundation. The year 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of Eugene V. Debs’ death in 1926. “2026 is the hundredth anniversary of Eugene V. Debs’ death,” Phillips said. “You know, it’s significant, I think, as a historian, about what was happening a hundred years ago—and to celebrate his accomplishments during his lifetime.” Today, the Eugene V. Debs Home and Museum houses many of his personal belongings, offering visitors an intimate look at the legacy he left behind. Beyond his union leadership, Debs was a major political figure of his era. “I think it’s significant for all of us that live in Terre Haute, who are from Terre Haute, to just think about the fact that this was a five-time presidential candidate,” Phillips added. title: ‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea - The Guardian
content: Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved a dozen incidents and two arrests The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger. Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly. Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”. “Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.” Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty. Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him. Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS. The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”. Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says. Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’” Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving. Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment. Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes. “We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says. The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag. Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says. Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach. Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse. “We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’” The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals. For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end. For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety. Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’” An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs. Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents. But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

title: Queen Mary reveals her special bond with Harald V in her first engagement after his death: “He was Norway’s grandfather” - HOLA
content: Europe’s royal families are mourning the loss of a man who, for them, was a true role model. For thirty-five years, King Harald was the example that new generations of royals looked up to, a sovereign whose reign was defined, among other things, by the warmth and closeness he showed in each of his public appearances. His absence will be forever recorded in the pages of history and has unleashed a wave of emotion among today’s monarchies, who have not hesitated to express their feelings and their love for the late King. It was Queen Mary, during one of her first engagements after his passing, who chose to speak from the heart to reveal the closeness she shared with Haakon of Norway’s father, a gesture that King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands has echoed from afar, continuing this tribute of affection. It’s no secret that the Scandinavian royal families share a deep affection for one another, a bond that has endured over the centuries and is often reflected in the history books that bring these ties to life today. On several occasions, King Harald V offered guidance to the then Crown Princess, now Queen of Denmark. “Harald was a very good person. It has always been a special pleasure to be in his company,” Mary of Denmark said, her emotion visible in her eyes. She spoke these sincere words just before beginning the first official engagement on her schedule since the King’s death, which made the moment all the more symbolic. “I completely understand why he was known as Norway’s grandfather, because he always had eyes for everyone,” recalled the wife of Frederik X. With these words, she wanted to highlight the love the Norwegian people have shown their King in recent days. Outside Oslo’s Royal Palace, an immense garden of flowers has sprung up, growing day by day as a powerful symbol of the deep affection so many felt for the monarch. “I was able to experience that love myself: his great care and concern,” she said, fighting to hold back her emotions. Speaking to the media, she also recalled her first meeting with the King, underscoring that the respect she felt for Harald went far beyond the fact that they shared the same position. At the same time, she extended her thoughts to the new sovereigns, Haakon VIII and Mette-Marit, “The new royal couple knows that our thoughts are with them during this time of change and that, of course, they have our full support.” After these moving remarks, the Queen continued with her duties, taking part in the program organized for Denmark’s National Business Day, visiting companies and different locations to immerse herself in this period of innovation. Later, Frederik X’s wife presented the Danish Business Award 2026, putting the finishing touch on a day in which all words of affection were directed toward Norway’s Royal Court. With this gesture, Queen Mary once again strengthened those ties, sending all her love to the new court ahead of her trip. As was confirmed just a few days ago, the King and Queen of Denmark will attend the State Funeral of Harald V of Norway on September 9, where they will be joined by King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima, as well as Princess Beatrix and Princess Amalia of the Netherlands, the King and Queen of Belgium, the entire Swedish royal family, and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess of Japan, heirs to the Chrysanthemum Throne. © ¡HOLA! title: V’ghn, 450 among first performers announced for Caribbean Music Awards - Caribbean National Weekly
content: The Caribbean Music Awards has announced the first wave of performers for its fourth annual ceremony, set for Saturday, September 19, at the National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago. V’ghn, Freetown Collective, Jah Mason, 450, 1T1 and Theomaa are among the artists slated to perform, representing a mix of soca, reggae, dancehall, bouyon and contemporary Caribbean sounds. “The lineup reflects the depth of a region where distinct musical traditions continue to evolve, intersect and find new audiences around the world, with each artist bringing a distinct voice and perspective to the NAPA stage,” organizers said. Several of the performers are also nominees at this year's awards. V’ghn earned seven nominations, while Freetown Collective received three. 1T1 is recognized in the bouyon categories, 450 is nominated for Dancehall Album of the Year and Theomaa is up for Bouyon Song of the Year. Additional performers, presenters and special appearances are expected to be announced ahead of the ceremony. This year's awards will also spotlight Dominica as the birthplace of bouyon, a genre that organizers say has gained an increasingly prominent place in Caribbean and international music. “From carnival celebrations across the Caribbean to Fête de la Musique and beyond, Bouyon has become a defining sound of celebration, bringing new audiences to the genre while keeping its Dominican roots firmly in view,” organizers said. The Government of Dominica, through the Ministry of Tourism and the Discover Dominica Authority, will participate as a category sponsor as part of efforts to promote the country's music and culture. “As the genre continues to evolve, Dominica remains at the forefront of efforts to preserve, celebrate and elevate the cultural traditions that gave Bouyon its foundation,” organizers said. The ceremony marks a new chapter for the Caribbean Music Awards, with Trinidad and Tobago becoming the first Caribbean destination to host the event as organizers seek to highlight different islands and their cultural traditions in future editions. Billboard has also joined this year's event as the Official Global Media Partner and will livestream the Caribbean Music Awards red carpet special while promoting the event across its digital and social platforms. Organizers said the partnership will give international audiences “a front-row look” at the artists, honorees and cultural figures attending the ceremony while bringing the energy of Trinidad to Billboard's global music audience. TRACE will return as a media partner, extending coverage of the awards across the Caribbean, France and African territories through its international music and culture platforms. The awards will form part of the inaugural Caribbean Elite Weekend Experience, scheduled for September 18-20 across Trinidad and Tobago. The weekend will begin with a welcome reception on Friday, September 18, followed by the Caribbean Music Awards on Saturday. The festivities will conclude Sunday with the Stars & Steel Concert & Awards. This year's ceremony will be hosted by Trinidadian singer Nailah Blackman and comedian Majah Hype. Shyne, Calypso Rose, Alan Cavé and Patra will also be honored for their contributions to Caribbean music and culture. The event is presented by Tourism Trinidad Limited, with support from the Tobago Tourism Agency Limited, the Ministry of Trade, Investment and Tourism, and Global Trinidad and Tobago. title: The Last V8 Manual Sedan Has 4 Months Left. Act Now. - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update The Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing is the last V8 manual rear-wheel-drive four-door sedan sold in America, and it has four months left. Production for the entire CT5 range ends in December 2026, and for buyers who have been watching the used market, that clock matters more than it might seem. End-of-production announcements have a predictable effect on used-car pricing: dealers hold asking prices firm, private sellers test premiums, and the window for a fair deal quietly closes. The Blackwing's combination of genuine scarcity, strong value retention, and a final-year limited edition signal that this repricing may already be underway. The recipe the Blackwing follows — supercharged V8, three pedals, rear-wheel drive, four doors — used to have company. The E39 and F10 BMW M5, the E90 M3, the Chevrolet SS, and the Pontiac G8 all fit that brief. Even Dodge's four-door Charger dropped the manual entirely before its latest generation arrived. In 2026, the Blackwing stands alone. What makes that more striking is the spec it carries into extinction. The supercharged 6.2-liter LT4 V8 produces 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque, routed exclusively to the rear axle through a Tremec TR6060 six-speed with No-Lift Shift and Active Rev-Matching. While BMW, Mercedes-AMG, and Porsche have spent the better part of a decade pairing comparable outputs with all-wheel drive, Cadillac never touched the front axle. The manual survived the 2025 facelift on the strength of a nearly 50-percent take rate among buyers in 2023 — a number that speaks for itself. For its final year, Cadillac introduced the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series, marking the brand's first U.S. Grand Prix. A revised supercharger pushes output to 685 horsepower and 673 lb-ft of torque. Only 26 units will be built. That production number is less a car and more a market signal. When a manufacturer closes out a model with a 26-unit special edition, it confirms that the standard car's era is genuinely ending — and it sets a precedent for how limited editions from the same run will be valued at auction. Earlier limited runs have already demonstrated the pattern: the 2022 First Edition (250 units) and the 2023 120th Anniversary Edition (120 units) both command premiums over standard Blackwing asking prices today. The Blackwing has held value unusually well for a modern performance sedan. The 2022 model launched at a base MSRP of $83,995. Kelley Blue Book currently lists a fair purchase price of $76,250 — roughly a 10-percent decline over four years. For context, a typical new car loses closer to 40 to 50 percent of its value in the same window. That retention rate reflects genuine demand, not just enthusiast sentiment. The 2026 base price has risen to $98,900 before destination, which widens the gap between new and used — but that gap is what buyers should be watching closely. As the December production cutoff approaches, used asking prices on platforms like Autotrader and Carvana tend to drift upward as sellers anchor to replacement cost rather than depreciated value. Certified pre-owned inventory through Cadillac dealers adds another layer: CPO premiums are already baked into asking prices, and those premiums typically expand when a model goes out of production and warranty-backed supply dries up. Cadillac has confirmed the CT5 will return with gasoline engines. On whether a Blackwing version comes back, the company has said nothing. That silence is the operative fact for used buyers: there is no successor announced, no replacement spec confirmed, and no timeline for a follow-up manual V8 sedan from any American brand. For a buyer who has been waiting for prices to soften further, the calculus has shifted. The combination of a confirmed end date, a 26-unit final edition, and a track record of limited-run premiums suggests that the used market floor is closer to where it is now than where it might go in six months. Acting before dealer inventory tightens and private-seller expectations reset is the straightforward read. Whether that means pulling the trigger on a CPO 2023 or targeting a clean 2022 First Edition before auction season picks it up, the four-month window is the relevant frame. We want to hear from you. title: Canonical Evolution of Enterprise Open Source RISC-V at Hot Chips 2026 - ServeTheHome
content: Canonical presented the Evolution of Enterprise Open Source RISC-V at Hot Chips 2026. Gordan Markuš, Canonical’s Director of Silicon Alliances, walked through how Ubuntu is built, how ISA support is managed across architectures, and what it will take to make RISC-V enterprise-ready. We did this one live like our other Hot Chips coverage, but are publishing it a bit later around a cluster of RISC-V pieces. Canonical’s underlying argument is that an Ubuntu system should behave like an Ubuntu system no matter what processor drives it. Its presentation builds from how Ubuntu packages are assembled and supported, then applies that model to RISC-V. Ubuntu is assembled from a kernel and user space that Canonical commits to supporting for years. This Universe package archive contains roughly 30,000 packages, while the smaller Main archive contains about 3,000 packages and offers a longer support window, up to 15 years with Ubuntu Pro. Canonical also maintains a portfolio of kernels tuned for hyperscaler and silicon partners, which matters for RISC-V because there is no single reference design. The core aim is for an Ubuntu system to always behave like an Ubuntu system, regardless of the ISA or platform. Canonical says its work is not done until it can long-term patch and maintain the released binary aggregation and deliver a unified Ubuntu experience, meaning every new architecture has to flow through the same release and maintenance cycle. Packages are built for each supported architecture, and each architecture gets a baseline, the oldest or least capable ISA and extension set that can run Ubuntu of that generation. Canonical provides server resources for building and distributing packages and maintains a core development team responsible for their upkeep. RISC-V may sound exotic, but Ubuntu supports not only Arm and x86 CPUs but also IBM POWER and Z mainframes. Canonical shows where each architecture baseline sits today. This amd64 target assumes the original 64-bit AMD and Intel CPUs, while arm64 uses an ARMv8-A baseline with VFPv4 and NEON. This RISC-V riscv64 target moved from the RVA20 profile to the RVA23 profile with Ubuntu 25.10. Beyond baselines, Ubuntu 25.10 introduced architecture variants, allowing packages to be built more than once, each targeting different CPU features. This amd64v3 variant targets the x86-64-v3 microarchitecture level, adding instructions such as AVX2, FMA, and BMI2 while retaining support for older machines. This is the same pattern Canonical plans to apply to future RISC-V profiles. If you saw the Update on RISC-V Standards and Adoption at Hot Chips 2026, the motivation will make sense. Ubuntu introduced arm64 support back in 2011, but really it was Ubuntu 16.04 LTS that made Arm server CPUs usable without lots of custom patching. It wants to support advanced features and platform-specific acceleration on new ISAs without weakening security and support SLAs. RVA23 is the standardized application baseline Canonical is targeting for 64-bit application processors. Since it requires vector operations, hypervisor support, and bit manipulation out of the box, RVA23 aims to deliver binary portability across diverse silicon and remove software porting ambiguity. The RVA23 profile ratification is done, and so is server platform ratification, with server-class RVA23 hardware expected from multiple vendors in 2026 and 2027. Canonical notes that unlocking a new major profile is non-trivial, since its build systems require upgrades and cross-team coordination. Profiles help ensure that hardware implementer roadmaps and software developer roadmaps can intersect. Package coverage on RISC-V is close to catching up with the mainstream builds. Around 95% of packages are currently available on RISC-V compared with amd64, while Snap support is still a work in progress because most publicly available snaps today target the client and desktop ecosystem. Our STH team generally prefers to use the more generic apt package manager rather than snaps, but here we are. With 3,443 packages under test and 1,898 passing, RISC-V posts about a 55.1 percent pass rate on an Ubuntu 26.10 test snapshot, well below the roughly 92 percent seen on amd64. Canonical attributes part of that to emulated build and test targets, stretching execution times from hours to days, and to adding native RISC-V builders with help from partners supplying server-grade RVA23 platforms. It also has a much lower percentage of packages that have tests than the other architectures, which gives you a good idea of just how mature RISC-V is. Canonical Kubernetes and MicroCloud are being ported for native RISC-V container orchestration and edge cloud. The company is working on bringing RISC-V out across its stack though. Open source collaboration is central to the push. Canonical participates in the RISE Project with RISC-V International, which targets commercial software readiness across mobile, consumer electronics, datacenter, and automotive. RISE focuses on accelerating open-source software for RISC-V, improving platform implementation quality, and aligning ecosystem efforts. Native RISC-V runners on Ubuntu 24.04 back a build and board farm hosted at Scaleway Elastic Metal with Alibaba and SpacemiT hardware, and the project reports 24,000 jobs and 700,000 minutes across 116 organizations. Taken together, Canonical is betting that standardized profiles and broad upstream collaboration can push RISC-V past the software readiness gap that has historically slowed open source adoption of new ISAs. It frames RVA23-style profiles as the way to make software targeting predictable and to make multi-architecture maturity the foundation for enterprise-grade deployments. With server-class RVA23 hardware arriving over the next two years, the software stack now has a fixed target to converge on. Hopefully this moves RISC-V into a more mainstream role. title: Virginia Women’s Soccer Fails to Impress v Georgetown - Sports Illustrated
content: I’m writing this at 10:30 on Monday morning.  I was traveling over the weekend, so I got around to watching this game late anyway, but truth be told, I still haven’t yet thought of what to say about this game.  There was nothing wrong about the game, nothing glaring about the team’s performance.  There was also nothing particularly noteworthy about the game either.  I took three pages of notes, and half of my notes were just noting the substitutions.   This was a rather dour game. Georgetown, for their part, had scheduled a heavy dose of the ACC for their non-conference slate, having already played Stanford (a 2 – 0 loss) and Virginia Tech (a 2 – 1 loss) before Virginia.  Georgetown’s best player, and probably the overall player of the match, was keeper Reiley Fitzpatrick who was successful in defending a pair of one-v-one breakaways.  Fitzpatrick was also very quick off her line snuffing out multiple long ball, over the back line, Virginia attacks. And going over the top was clearly central to the Virginia game plan because Aniya Collier got the start at center forward in the absence of Sophia Bradley (who was nowhere to be seen). Collier does have speed, and she got two shots off of long balls, but most of the long balls played were just that- too long.  Long, over-the-top balls, even if they don’t succeed in springing Collier or wingbacks Carrie Helfrich and Liv Rademaker, can be useful if they can pull the defense out of shape, but that never happened.  Georgetown was, to borrow Steven Swanson’s favorite term when praising an opponent, “organized,” and the Cavaliers never really came close to breaking down the Hoyas. Swanson made two changes to his starters entering the game: as noted, Collier got the start at striker, and Liv Rademaker replaced Faith Broering amongst the back three.  It is still early in the season, but both Helfrich and Kyra Koopman both seem more incisive on the right side, and with Rademaker playing centrally, both spent time on the left wing. And that was part of the problem with this game; many players just seemed off.  Teams win games when their stars play like stars, their good players play above themselves, and their role players are impactful when they come in.  None of which happened yesterday.  Helfrich was ineffective on the left; Addison Halpern never got into a rhythm; Sarah Flammia and Kyndal Shuler, who both provided a spark when they entered vs Tennessee, were sparkless against Georgetown.  Jordyn Hardeman got her pocket picked on at least four occasions, and Allie Ross was largely anonymous.  Both teams struggled to get into a rhythm, as there could easily have been 25 throw-ins in the first 25 minutes of the game. Georgetown closed out the first half on a trot, dominating play for the last 10 minutes with a high-degree-of-difficulty one-v-one from a wide angle and a lovely bullet cross that had it found a Hoya would have been in the back of the net.  But Georgetown is looking like a mid-table Big East team at the moment, and couldn’t convert. Virginia, as is becoming a regular thing, came out on the front foot in the second half, and, well, they had their chances.  Hardeman had a lovely shot that keeper Fitzpatrick parried wide, and she got up quickly enough to deflect the follow-up shot.  A corner found Rademaker unmarked on the back post, but the ball got stuck between her feet, and she couldn’t convert.  Halpern had a one-on-one with the keeper, dribbled around her, but couldn’t get the shot off, and Georgetown’s defense covered up, denying her, and then Ross, what should have been an empty-net goal. Ella Carter, who is becoming the embodiment of a second-half player, twice led a couple of counter-attacks but would end up holding on to the ball for a dribble too long.  One of those times Ross was offside, and the other time Collier had to stop her run, or she would have been offside.   The ball simply has to be played much faster.  And Carter wasn’t alone.  On two other occasions, I found myself mumbling at the screen, “Now.   Now!” There were really only two highlights for a veteran observer of the women’s team.  One was seeing the continued growth of Kathryn Kelly, who is, for the first time in her five years, getting real minutes.  She’s a solid defender who understands positioning and using her body, which she did repeatedly against the much faster Abby Droner.  Guile winning out over athleticism is one of the reasons why I watch sport. And the second is watching Koopman when someone tries to dribble her.  Koop’s back leg is maybe the best foot on this entire soccer team.  It’s only been six games now, but I feel like she’s the best on-ball defender I’ve seen in my decade of covering Virginia women’s soccer. So, when the highlights of a game are Kelly’s positioning and Koopman’s dribble stuffing, that is probably all you need to know about the game. The Verdict:  One hundred and eighty minutes of soccer against Tennessee and Georgetown produced just a single goal.  Goals are going to be hard to come by, at least for as long as Gio Canali is in Poland for the U20 Women’s World Cup. Next Up:  Virginia travels to Winston-Salem to take on Wake Forest on Saturday, September 12th.  Game time is 7:00pm and can be seen on ACC Network Extra.  Wake is on a roll: until defeating #21 Florida in Gainesville 2 – 1, they had not allowed a goal in their first six games.  There might be more room at the top of the ACC this year.  Notre Dame has had some injury issues and Florida State and UNC both seem “off” this year.  Wake is very much on an upward trajectory the past four years, and I know they know that.  Getting a win against Virginia in the ACC’s opening week would be a heck of a statement.  How is Virginia going to handle the pressure? Val graduated from the University of Virginia in the last millennium, back when writing one's senior thesis by hand was still a thing. The match will be streamed live from 16:00 on inter.it, the official Inter app, Inter TV and the Inter 24/7 FAST channel. MATCHDAY 1 - Tuesday 8 September 2026, 16:00Real Madrid vs Inter MATCHDAY 2 - Tuesday 13 October 2026, 15:00Inter vs Club Brugge MATCHDAY 3 - Wednesday 21 October 2026, 16:00Inter vs Shakhtar Donetsk MATCHDAY 4 - Tuesday 3 November 2026, 14:00Feyenoord vs Inter MATCHDAY 5 - Wednesday 25 November 2026, 15:00Inter vs Stuttgart MATCHDAY 6 - Wednesday 9 December 2026, 16:00Borussia Dortmund vs Inter As in previous seasons, the Youth League begins with two separate paths: one aligned with the Champions League League Phase and another featuring the domestic champions from UEFA's 52 member associations. The Champions League path features the youth teams of all 36 clubs competing in Europe's premier club competition, including Inter Primavera. The league phase mirrors the first six matchdays of the Champions League League Phase, with the same fixtures played across both competitions: three at home and three away. The top 22 teams will progress to the round of 32, with the draw scheduled for Friday 11 December. The domestic champions path features 50 teams and is played over three two-legged knockout rounds. The ten sides that emerge from the third qualifying round will secure a place in the Youth League round of 32. From the round of 32 onwards, the competition moves into a single-leg knockout format. A new open draw will be held for the round of 16. As usual, the tournament will culminate in a four-team final stage featuring the semi-finals and final. The result moved the Nerazzurri onto seven points, following an opening-day victory away to Genoa, sealed by Carrara, and a frustrating 2-2 draw against Empoli at the KONAMI Women & Talent Center. Bigica's side now face reigning champions Real Madrid, who lifted the trophy last season after defeating Club Brugge on penalties following a 1-1 draw in the final. Real Madrid v Inter, the Nerazzurri's opening fixture of the 2026/27 UEFA Youth League League Phase, kicks off at 16:00 on Tuesday 8 September. title: A G-Wagen With a Corvette Heart: Driving Expedition Motor Company’s V-8-Powered Wolf 620GE - motortrend.com
content: This 1991 Mercedes-Benz 250GD got the restomod of a lifetime—and we had a ball driving it. “If you pull in front of the white Countach, I will see you.” It’s one of the best text messages I’ve ever received, a sign of good things to come. I’m at Monterey Car Week where I’m picking up Paul Stehn, product director for Expedition Motor Company (EMC), in our long-term Subaru Outback Wilderness for a short drive to the parking lot of his hotel to get behind the wheel of a far more robust off-road machine: the Expedition Motor Company Wolf 620GE. Based on a 1991 Mercedes-Benz 250GD, a diesel-powered military version of the G-Class SUV from the code-named W461 generation, this China Blue EMC Wolf 620GE has gone through a 100-point restoration that sees the 4x4 torn down to the frame and rebuilt via a 2,500-man-hour process involving a team of 26 craftspeople. Eager to cosplay as a well-to-do participant in one of the most premier automotive events on the calendar, I slide behind the two-spoke steering wheel of the Wolf and set off with Stehn sitting shotgun ready to answer my burning questions about this LS3-swapped machine. EMC’s founder, Alex Levin, didn’t originally set out to equip the company’s restomods with anything other than the original OM602 diesel engine outfitted to the Mercedes-Benz 250GD, but customer demand has led EMC to offer the Wolf with the turbocharged OM605a engine that makes 225 hp and 300 lb-ft of torque and the higher-output OM606a turbodiesel, which develops 275 hp and 350 lb-ft of torque. Now there’s also an LS3 V-8 with 6.2 liters of displacement on offer, hence the clever 620GE naming and badging. The eight-cylinder powerplant cranks out 430 hp and 425 lb-ft of torque, essentially the same figures it made when it was originally outfitted to the C6 Chevrolet Corvette. A six-speed 6L806 automatic transmission sends power to the part-time four-wheel-drive system. Some things in life are inevitable: death, taxes, and traffic during Monterey Car Week. With that in mind, you’ll understand my apprehension-tempered excitement to drive a restomod worth over a quarter of a million dollars into the fray of supercar drivers and influencers. Fortunately, the EMC  Wolf 620GE’s powertrain has been tuned to handle real life. Thanks to EMC’s fettling, the LS3 has a relaxed feel that suits the SUV’s droptop body style. The Wolf happily idles through beach towns like Monterey and comfortably navigates the twisty roads of Pebble Beach’s famous 17 Mile Drive without exceeding 25 mph. However, when you do step on it, the V-8’s grunt reveals itself, rocketing you up to highway speeds without straining. As for the transmission, the 6L806 behaves about as well as you’d expect. It’s neither sharp nor dimwitted, supplying well-timed shifts with good spacing between the gears. The balanced setup suits the overall character of this beach-cruising G-Wagen. The steering is quite heavy in its feel on turn-in, but the wide-diameter tiller provides lots of leverage. Despite the heft from the power-steering rack, the Wolf is maneuverable at lower speeds and tracks accurately on the freeway, far better than what I would expect from a classic SUV. What’s more, the absence of shuddering and jittering over road surfaces is a testament to EMC’s high build-quality standards. As we wind through the curves of 17 Mile Drive, Stehn lets me know that the Wolf’s optionally equipped Fox suspension was set to a firmer setting for our drive. The intention is to firm up the ride to control body roll on the street. For those taking the Wolf off-road, this configuration would be too stiff. Instead, the Fox shocks would need to be loosened up to allow for more compliance while traversing imperfections and obstacles. Getting closer to the cliffside of Pebble Beach, I note that our drive route covers basics of what I suspect an owner would experience operating their Wolf. While driving through the upscale neighborhoods of Pacific Grove Acres, the 620GE is very compliant and obedient. EMC’s throttle mapping makes gentle starts a cinch, and the exhaust note hums at a volume that won’t disturb the peninsula’s well-to-do residents. Enthusiasts needn’t worry that this Wolf is always docile, though. As soon as I get clear of the houses, I indulge in a pull. The G-Wagen’s exhaust is acceptably loud, and it sounds like a true naturally aspirated American V-8. EMC seems to have gotten the formula right for what restomod shoppers need in their rig. We blend right in with the traffic along the Pebble Beach coast. Thrumming alongside the water, the China Blue G-Wagen looks at home with its eye-popping paint, 18-inch Astaroth wheels, and contrasting Chestnut interior. If we had the top on, it would have been a luxurious shade of beige, but we’re happy to soak up the sun and the cool air of California’s Central Coast. Parking up at a scenic overlook, we take some time to admire the Wolf 620GE’s finer details. Inside the cabin, there’s AAA European oak trim, a small display with wireless Apple CarPlay, a Harman Kardon sound system, air conditioning, and heated seating for both rows. EMC does a good job adding modern livability to the Wolf without degrading its vintage looks; as a clever touch, the USB ports are hidden beneath a cover that looks like it’s for the cigarette lighter. These features come at no cost, but there’s a ton of other customization options available for the Wolf. Stehn shows us a bunch of the swatches for the soft-top fabric and leathers for the seats. On the outside, our test car has a China Blue jerry can matching the body color. Other upgrades cost extra. Equipped on our test car is a bullbar for $2,500, EMC running board side steps for $2,500, third-row inward seats for $3,000, and the Fox suspension we mentioned earlier costs $4,700. EMC has left some features off our build, as well. You can also get an EMC winch bumper with a Warn winch for $4,500, headlamp guards for $350, and Baja Designs 3-inch pod lights for $750. After taking in the view of both the ocean and EMC’s creation, I fire up the Wolf 620GE and give it a rev for MotorTrend’s social media before getting out of Dodge. A Car Week miracle, the way back is devoid of any other vehicles, allowing me to drive the open-air G-Wagen with a bit more enthusiasm. Having now worked up some confidence in the 35-year-old SUV, I find it easy to place the wheels where I want them on the road. The throttle responds with the exact amount of power I want when accelerating out of a turn. Even though the Wolf 620GE has the brakes from a Mercedes-Benz AMG G55, this is the biggest point of adjustment compared to driving modern SUVs. The brakes are more than capable of bringing the three-ton Wolf to a halt, but you really have to press down on the pedal to get the calipers to bite. Over the drive, I was startled a few times because I needed to squeeze down farther than expected to get proper stopping power. I’m sure this is something you’d get used to if you drove the 620GE regularly, but a bit more firmness in the pedal would be welcome. After making our way out of 17 Mile Drive, we face a final challenge: threading some tricky roundabouts choked with fast-moving traffic. At this point, I’m feeling confident behind the wheel of the Wolf, and we circulate with ease. It doesn’t take much to get the hang of EMC’s creation; both enthusiasts and those who just think the Wolf looks cool will be comfortable behind the wheel. The Wolf steams to 65 mph with a roar of its V-8, overtaking slow-moving traffic like a G-Wagen that rolled out of the factory yesterday. On the highway back to basecamp, we sail along, marveling at our good fortune for a beautiful day absent from difficulty. The Wolf hasn’t stuttered or creaked through the entire drive at any speed. Parting with EMC’s Stehn, I’m left feeling satisfied; restomods seldom require so little effort to enjoy. In a world of far pricier restomod SUVs, where Ford Broncos built by Icon can easily reach $300,000 and rigs re-engineered by Velocity Restorations can hit the $450,000 mark, a turnkey G-Wagen with a V-8 like the EMC Wolf 620GE is a relative bargain. Pricing begins at $252,000 absent of the options mentioned earlier, with the final sticker price of this China Blue G-Wagen totaling $265,550. Not only is the LS3-powered Wolf a cohesive product, but EMC doesn’t require you to bring it a chassis. Stehn tells us EMC has roughly 150 classic G-Wagens ready to go for when it’s time to start a build. If a quarter of a million dollars sounds too steep, you can skip the V-8 and save tens of thousands of dollars on any of the other engine options. A restomod’s purpose is to combine vintage charm with modern usability, and EMC has nailed the brief with the Wolf 620GE. The boxy ute gets smiles from onlookers, and you enjoy classic car privilege when you’re behind the wheel. Still, you don’t have to go without the creature comforts that have become normal in the three and a half decades since the W461 went into production. Perhaps most important, the Wolf is right at home next to supercars like the Lamborghini Countach at the valet during Monterey Car Week. 1991 Mercedes-Benz 250GD Wolf 620GE by EMC Specifications Get the newest car reviews, hottest auto news, and expert analysis of the latest trends delivered straight to your inbox! title: A New Genocide Convention Case in the ICJ: DRC v Rwanda Version 3.0 - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists [Melanie O’Brien is Professor of International Law and Deputy Head of School (Research) at the University of Western Australia Law School, and visiting scholar with the University of Minnesota Law School’s Human Rights Center. Thomas Shacklock is the research director of Crane Center for Mass Atrocity Prevention, a research contributor at the Human Rights Research Center, and a nonprofit consultant at Dragonfly Consulting Group. He is soon starting a PhD in Politics at King’s College London, where he will focus on conflict and peacebuilding.] In June 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) started proceedings against Rwanda at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing its neighbour of responsibility for genocide and other crimes on its territory since the 1990s. This is the third ICJ case the DRC has brought against Rwanda since the 1990s, having filed unsuccessful cases in 1999 and 2002. This post will provide a background of the conflict in the DRC, and then an overview of the DRC’s ICJ cases against Rwanda, with a focus on this new application, aka DRC v Rwanda Version 3.0. Conflicts in the DRC are complex. There are currently over 120 armed groups in eastern DRC, which is characterised by an absent state. These armed groups have tended to generate income through the extraction of natural mineral resources, among other income sources, since the Second Congo War (1997-2003). Yet, mineral exploitation is generally not the main driver of conflicts in eastern DRC, which often stem from a complex interplay of intercommunity land struggles, exclusionary politics, other ethnic-based grievances, and the security, geopolitical, or economic interests of neighbouring states. Various Congolese elites and neighbouring countries have been responsible for fuelling violent conflicts, committing serious atrocities, and exploiting resources, with numerous countries intervening in the Congo Wars (1996-2003). However, Rwanda’s interventions are a particularly salient issue in Congolese politics. Over the years, Uganda and Burundi have intervened due to their economic, security, or geostrategic interests. The current M23 conflict even appears to have been sparked by Rwanda seeing its economic interests threatened by Uganda expanding its own in eastern DRC. Burundi has also been supporting the Congolese military in the M23 conflict. Despite the complex roles of these different actors, the DRC’s case focuses on atrocities perpetrated by Rwanda, alleging that they have been aimed at destroying Hutu and other ethnic communities, particularly the Nyindu, at least in part. Other communities mentioned include the Bembe, Lega, Nande, Hunde, and Bashi. The case lists a range of atrocities, which may or may not be linked to “genocidal acts,” to which these communities have been subjected, including mass killings, forced displacement, sexual violence, torture, and other forms of inhuman and degrading treatment. Given the entrenched violence and insecurity in the region, eastern DRC has had a large and long-standing peacekeeping presence, first in the form of MONUC (1999-2010), and then in the form of MONUSCO (2010-present). Since 2023, a planned withdrawal of MONUSCO has been delayed by UN Security Council votes extending its mandate, but it has been formally completed in the eastern province of South Kivu. The UN still plays an important role in reporting on human rights abuses in the DRC, including those linked to Rwanda, having established an independent commission of inquiry to investigate atrocities in North and South Kivu in 2025. Since 1996, Rwanda has participated in cycles of conflict in the DRC either directly or through supporting armed rebellions. These rebellions include the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) in the First Congo War (1996-97) and the Congolese Rally for Democracy (RCD) during the Second Congo War (1998-2003). Rwanda backed another rebellion from 2006 to 2009, and the M23 insurgency (named after a peace deal signed on 23 March 2009) emerged from 2012 to 2013. M23 reemerged in 2021, forming part of a broader alliance called the Congo River Alliance (AFC) from 2023, and established a parallel administrative system in its occupied territories in eastern Congo. Throughout these periods, the UN and NGOs have documented serious atrocities committed by these groups against communities mentioned in the ICJ case. Rwandan interventions in the DRC are connected to the 1994 genocide committed by Rwandan Hutu extremists against Rwandan Tutsi (the Rwandan genocide). A primarily Tutsi rebellion, the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), ended that genocide and seized control of Rwanda. However, the RPF/AFDL massacred tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees who had fled into neighbouring DRC (then named ’Zaire’) while pursuing exiled genocide perpetrators. Ethnic identity is a dimension connecting these contexts. Hutu and Tutsi live across the wider Great Lakes region of Central Africa, being the two main communities in Rwanda and Burundi and minorities in the more ethnically diverse provinces of eastern DRC. Rwandan-backed rebellions have historically recruited fighters from Congolese Tutsi communities, including Banyamulenge based in South Kivu, who have often experienced discrimination and persecution as perceived non-indigenous “Rwandan” outsiders. The DRC’s case should be situated within decades of academic and public debates on competing claims of genocide concerning communities in Rwanda, eastern DRC, and Burundi, which are overshadowed by the 1994 Rwandan genocide. A 2010 UN report documenting human rights violations in the Congo from 1993 to 2003, known as the “Mapping Exercise” report, suggested that the RPF’s 1996-97 massacres of Hutu refugees in Congo may have constituted genocide, although it did not establish genocidal intent. Various scholars and observers have argued that, although the RPF atrocities in the 1990s were egregious, they cannot be equated with the genocide against Rwandan Tutsi in ways that reinforce a “double genocide” theory. In filing its case at the ICJ, the DRC is putting these arguments to the test in the legal realm while establishing a clear throughline linking Rwanda’s historic and ongoing atrocities in eastern DRC. The DRC even emphasises in the introduction of its case that its accusations against Rwanda do not aim to minimise the 1994 extermination of Rwandan Tutsi. The 1994 Rwandan genocide is generally considered a “textbook” case, as the Hutu extremists, driven by an exclusionary ideology, orchestrated a meticulously organised state campaign to annihilate the Tutsi and politically moderate Hutu following a period of anti-Tutsi persecution and hate speech. The RPF atrocities targeting Hutu were driven by distinct factors and occurred amid evolving conflict dynamics. At home, the post-genocide Rwandan government has promoted an ideology of interethnic unity that erases ethnic identity since the late 1990s, albeit in a repressive political environment reportedly characterised by anti-Hutu discrimination in practice. In Zaire, atrocities against Hutu in the 1990s appeared to be aimed at collective punishment and population control, and may have been further driven by a suspicion that the victims were associated with extremists and collectively posed an existential threat to Tutsi. This mentality appears to still inform M23 atrocities against Hutu civilians associated with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a DRC-based militia comprising former exiled Rwandan Hutu extremists. The resurgence of M23 has also led the DRC army to collaborate with abusive “Wazalendo” (“patriots”) militias and the FDLR (with which it has collaborated before) and triggered an exacerbation of violence and sometimes genocidal hate speech against Congolese Tutsi, which the DRC’s case ignores. Neither these complex dynamics of victimisation nor the one-sided nature of the DRC’s case discount its accusations against Rwanda. However, they underscore the limitations of relying on “textbook” understandings of contextual drivers of genocide when assessing the atrocities in question. These complexities also matter because Rwanda is likely to cite anti-Tutsi violence and the perceived threat posed by the FDLR in its legal defence. Rwanda and M23 have cited these issues throughout the conflict, with M23 claiming to defend Congolese Tutsi, even though these problems have been exacerbated by its resurgence. In June 2025, the DRC and Rwanda signed a peace agreement. In August 2026 (after the DRC’s filing of the ICJ case discussed here), the DRC and M23 agreed to pursue peace negotiations and set up a ceasefire monitoring mechanism. It remains to be seen whether this is successful, given that fighting has continued in Eastern DRC despite the 2025 ceasefire agreement. The DRC has twice previously lodged claims against Rwanda in the ICJ. The first attempt was in 1999, brought under various treaties against Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda. In 2001, the case was discontinued against Burundi and Rwanda. It is worth mentioning that the case went on to become the well-known Armed Activities on the Territory of the Congo (Democratic Republic of the Congo v. Uganda) case, within which the ICJ held Uganda responsible for unlawful use of force and military intervention (occupation) in the DRC, and that Uganda had violated a variety of international humanitarian and human rights law obligations. This case was about the conduct of the Ugandan armed forces but also the military, logistic, economic and financial support that Uganda provided to non-state armed groups in the DRC, all of whom were responsible for the unlawful conduct. Like the Rwandan interventions, this case too was related to the abundant natural resources in the DRC. This was worth mentioning because the parallels with the case against Rwanda are substantial, and a strong indicator that the DRC is likely to be successful in the new case. The second attempt at a case against Rwanda was lodged in 2002, alleging ‘massive, serious and flagrant violations of human rights and international humanitarian law’. This case was again brought under a number of treaties, all of which the Court denied jurisdiction for various procedural reasons. At the time of submission, Rwanda had a reservation to Article IX of the Genocide Convention, which the ICJ found to be still active and therefore Rwanda did not consent to the ICJ’s jurisdiction over disputes under that treaty. The same reason was given for rejecting the claim under the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination (ICERD) (Rwanda’s reservation to Article 22). Both of those provisions were the compromissory clauses of those respective conventions. Jurisdiction under the other treaties in the claim, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), was likewise dismissed for the reason that none of the preconditions to the ICJ process required by those treaties had been met. On 26 June 2026, the DRC lodged a third application with the ICJ. This application alleges violations of the Genocide Convention, ICERD, CEDAW, and, unlike the 2002 application, the Convention Against Torture (CAT). The DRC is not invoking other treaties that were part of the previous claim (which includes claims under a wide variety of subject-matter treaties). This claim is much more focused and thematically structured. In this third case, the DRC claims that Rwanda, through the Rwandan Defence Force (RDF) and multiple militias working in collaboration with the RDF and Kigali’s leadership, is responsible for multiple violations of the listed treaties. Applying the Nicaragua test (Nicaragua paras. 109-110), the DRC’s claims are based on the structural dependence of the non-state actors on Kigali and on the effective control that Rwanda has over these armed groups (para. 144). The application sets out some basic facts (section II, pp. 6-34), noting that a full argument with more details will be provided if the case progresses to the merits stage. The facts set out the different phases of the conflict in the DRC, separating the facts across five periods of time from 1996 until today. This demonstrates the changes in non-state armed groups as participants in conflict. It also manifests the consistency of the types of violence across the periods. Massacres, sexual violence, forced displacement and torture in particular stand out as consistently committed across the decades. This section extensively references reports by UN bodies and NGOs, which indicates the type of evidence that the DRC will undoubtedly use to make its argument at the merits stage. The application then engages in its arguments about the Court’s competence, which in this case is crucial, given the 2002 application was rejected in full for competence reasons. Indeed, the DRC has been strategic with this case. In the years since the 2006 rejection of their second claim, the DRC acted to ensure that the procedural barriers that prevented the Court’s jurisdiction in the 2002 claim under the human rights treaties were overcome. Under Article 29 of CEDAW and Article 30 of CAT, a dispute concerning each convention ‘which is not settled by negotiation’ must be submitted to arbitration. If the arbitration cannot be agreed upon within six months, then one of the parties can refer the dispute to the ICJ. The DRC has ensured that this procedure has been followed. It has clearly raised issues of dispute, including publicly in various UN bodies, and these steps are outlined in this application. This includes holding a Human Rights Council side event at the Palais des Nations calling on the international community to mobilise against these crimes, including genocide (para. 109). It also includes diplomatic actions: a series of three note verbales to the Rwandan Foreign Minister across 2025 and 2026, including attempts to launch negotiations, to which the DRC received no response (paras. 111, 122-125, 132-135, 139-142). All these note verbales engaged with allegations of violations of all four treaties at issue in this claim. Therefore, the DRC has, for this third iteration of its case, ensured that procedural barriers to the ICJ’s competence are overcome. In addition, Rwanda withdrew without conditions its reservation to Article IX of the Genocide Convention and to Article 22 of ICERD in December 2008, thus eliminating the procedural obstacle to the ICJ’s jurisdiction under those treaties. The application then progresses to the specific claims under each treaty. The most space is given to the claim under the Genocide Convention (paras. 149-156): that Rwanda, from 1996 until the present day, through non-state actor intermediaries as well as the RDF and through omissions of conduct, through a lack of any measures to prevent or repress genocidal acts committed in eastern DRC, has been and is committing violations of the Genocide Convention.  The DRC’s claim alleges comprehensive violations of the Genocide Convention, across Articles I to VI, covering failure to prevent and punish; the commission of, attempt and complicity in genocide; special intent to commit genocide; direct and public incitement to genocide; failure to adopt legislative and judicial measures to facilitate application of the Genocide Convention and to repress and punish crimes of genocide; and hindering inquiries from international entities such as the UN.  The application argues that the dolus specialis of genocide can be inferred from circumstances, that indirect proof can demonstrate such intention. With reference to International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and ICJ cases, the DRC argues that multiple criteria can potentially be evidence of genocidal intent, such as the systematic character and disproportionate nature of attacks.  These allegations of genocide specifically refer to the targeting, with intent to destroy, of ethnic groups, particularly Rwandan refugee Hutus and the Nyindus. Based on the erga omnes partes nature of the Genocide Convention, the DRC argues that the case is relevant but even stronger because it is the state in question that has been affected by violations of the Genocide Convention, which is perhaps a reference to the fact that other cases currently before the ICJ under the Genocide Convention are predominantly brought by states who are themselves not directly affected by the genocide(s) they are alleging. The claim under ICERD is brief (paras. 157-8), alleging the commission of racial discrimination, with the facts detailing specific targeting of Hutus and Congolese minority groups. The DRC alleges violations of multiple provisions of the ICERD, crossing the obligations to eliminate racial discrimination, prohibit racial superiority propaganda, eliminate racial discrimination in all areas of access to rights (across a wide variety of rights), provide effective remedies for violations, and adopt measures to combat prejudices. This claim is that Rwanda is systematically violating the rights under ICERD of ethnic Congolese communities. Under CEDAW, the claim (paras. 159-164) is that violence against women amounts to a violation of the prohibition of discrimination against women (which is consistent with the CEDAW Committee’s interpretation of the treaty in General Recommendation 19). The particular focus of this claim is on the systematic sexual violence committed against ethnic minority women by non-state armed groups. The sexual violence is presented as a weapon of war and domination, which constitutes a ‘grave, systematic and continuing violation of the Convention’. The DRC also alleges a context of ‘submission of women in conditions of a discriminatory and inhumane existence’. Finally, the allegations under CAT (paras. 165-170) claim the systematic commission of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, specifically by complicity in providing support for non-state armed groups. The claim lists a non-exhaustive list including summary executions, simulated executions, death threats, public humiliation, beatings, arbitrary detention, gang rapes, mutilation, forced labour and use of child soldiers, carried out in North and South Kivu. The DRC also alleges the obstruction or lack of cooperation with international inquiry mechanisms. A claim across all alleged treaty violations is the failure of Rwanda to prevent, investigate and punish allegations of crimes, and to provide reparations. This also specifically includes references to the obligation aut dedere aut judicare, found across Articles 5-8 of CAT. The DRC provides the example of Laurent Nkunda, who Rwanda refuses to extradite to the DRC for acts of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. This third attempt at bringing a case against Rwanda by the DRC finally has a chance at success. Given the Court’s findings in 2005 of international law violations against Uganda in essentially the same context, and given that this time, the barriers to the Court’s competence have been removed through removal of reservations or the DRC ensuring that precursor acts are complete, it can be surmised that this case will not only reach the merits stage but the DRC is likely to succeed in achieving a ruling against Rwanda at least with regards to some aspects of this case. What is different in this case from the DRC v Uganda case is the inclusion of claims under the Genocide Convention, the specific focusing of the case on human rights treaties, and the exclusion of claims of breaches of IHL and claims under other various treaties relating to regional or aviation obligations. Therefore, the case is not a direct parallel with the DRC v Uganda case. The narrow scope of the case, with the facts relating to overlapping claims across the four treaties, is also what provides the DRC with a good chance of success in its claim. While it is outside the scope of this blog post to go into detail, it is worth mentioning that in 2023, the DRC brought a case against Rwanda in the African Court of Human Rights (ACtHR) (the first inter-state case before the ACtHR). This case has differences from the ICJ case. Firstly, it alleges breaches of different treaties: the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on Women’s Rights, the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Secondly, the ACtHR case is only based on conflict from 2021, focusing on M23 and Rwanda. Thirdly, in a 2025 decision on admissibility and jurisdiction, the ACtHR determined that there was no need for the existence of a prior dispute, as required with the ICJ, therefore there was no procedural barrier to the case. A judgment in this case will be rendered well before one at the ICJ, so no doubt the ICJ will draw on the ACtHR finding in its deliberations. In both cases, the DRC has requested each court (inter alia) hold Rwanda responsible for violations of international law, to end the violations or withdraw its troops and support, and to provide reparations for damage. In the ICJ, the request to provide reparations for damages is focused on the state (para. 171) (as it was in DRC v Uganda); in the ACtHR, the request is to repair the damage to the state and the populations who are victims of the alleged violations. Therefore, the cases may have similarities in their findings, but also differences given the distinct treaties on which the claims are based and that the reparations structure will no doubt diverge between cases. The DRC is covering its bases with multiple claims in multiple courts, and with a likelihood of success in both these cases. DRC v Rwanda Version 3.0 is also another case now before the ICJ dealing with human rights treaties and the Genocide Convention, a growing trend that we are witnessing as the Court becomes more involved in human rights and international crimes (particularly genocide) disputes. The ICJ’s role as an interpreter and enforcer of laws designed to protect people is increasing. These cases will create a strong new body of jurisprudence around state accountability for human rights abuses and international crimes, and this new DRC v Rwanda case (along with the ACtHR case) will most likely contribute to that. title: Pick of the stats: Watford v Preston North End - Yahoo Sports
content: Watford are hoping to end a run of just one point from their past three Championship games when they meet Preston North End on Tuesday (19:45 BST). By contrast, Preston collected their first three points of the campaign and ended a four-game losing streak against Blackburn Rovers at the weekend. Watford have won just one of their past eight Championship games against Preston (D5 L2), a 5-1 away victory in December 2023. Preston are unbeaten in four league visits to Watford (W1 D3), this after losing three of their previous four prior (D1). Watford have only lost one of their past nine midweek (Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday) home games in the Championship (W5 D3), a 2-0 defeat by Ipswich in February last season. Preston could lose each of their first three away games of a league season for the first time since 2018-19 (first five). Preston's Paul Heckingbottom is unbeaten in five league meetings with Watford (W3 D2) since a 1-0 defeat while in charge of Sheffield United in August 2022.

title: Pick of the stats: Cardiff City v Stoke City - Yahoo Sports
content: Stoke City are hoping to make it three successive Championship wins when they visit Cardiff City on Tuesday evening (19:45 BST). The Bluebirds are seeking a first home win since returning to the second tier this season. Cardiff lost their last Championship game against Stoke City 1-0 in April 2025, but have not lost successive league games to the Potters since February 2008. Stoke are looking to win back-to-back away league games against Cardiff City for only the second time, after doing so in October 1999. Cardiff have drawn both of their home league games this season; only in 1977-78, 1990-91, 1999-00, and 2000-01 have they started a league campaign with draws in their first three home matches. Stoke have lost each of their past nine away league outings, their longest run in the Football League since losing 10 in a row in September 1952. Stoke are winless in nine away league games against newly-promoted opponents (D3 L6) since a 5-1 win at Sunderland in March 2023.

title: King Harald V remembered as Norway’s ‘Sports King’ in never-before-seen photo - HOLA
content: Following his passing on August 28 at the age of 89, the Royal House of Norway has paid a heartfelt tribute to the memory of King Harald V by sharing a never-before-seen photo from his younger years. In it, he appears handsome and smiling, with the strong presence that always defined him. These beautiful snapshots offer a glimpse of the monarch in his younger years, because “for many people, King Harald became known as the ‘Sports King’,” the palace shared alongside the images showing him in enviable physical shape. The monarch himself summed up his commitment to sports in 2017: “Fortunately, sports are such an important part of Norway that they also become a natural part of a king’s work.” Over the decades, King Harald was a constant presence at the legendary Holmenkollen event, Norwegian national championships, World Championships and Olympic Games, reflecting his deep passion for and knowledge of sports. King Harald himself was a high-level sailor who had the great honor of carrying the Norwegian flag at the opening ceremony of the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympic Games. His sailing career included many memorable achievements: in 1987, he and his crew were crowned world champions aboard the sailboat “Fram X,” and in 2005 they claimed the title of European champions with “Fram XV,” a passion that led him to compete in national and international regattas until 2022. After his death, the sports world came together to honor him. Quanhai Li, president of World Sailing, the organization for which the King served as honorary president after having led the Norwegian Sailing Federation in the 1970s, shared some moving words in his memory: “His Majesty King Harald V had a commanding presence on the water, where he raced alongside several generations of sailors, representing both his country and his sport with dignity and distinction.” “His commitment is a powerful reminder of the unique camaraderie that defines our sport, and everyone at World Sailing is deeply grateful for the support he gave us throughout his time as honorary president. His Majesty’s legacy will remain forever etched in this sport and in the hearts of sailors around the world. He will be deeply missed.” For its part, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued a statement expressing its sorrow: “The IOC is deeply saddened by the death of His Majesty King Harald V of Norway, a three-time Olympic sailor and Norway’s flag bearer at the Tokyo 1964 Olympic Games.” A great supporter of the Olympic Movement, King Harald V declared two editions of the Games open in Lillehammer: the Olympic Winter Games in 1994 and the Winter Youth Olympic Games in 2016. His legacy will continue to inspire generations across the Olympic world. Our deepest condolences go to his entire family and to the people of Norway.” © ¡HOLA!
